summary:
Lambayeque has no trans-specific ordinance, municipal rule or local enforcement pattern on record; a visitor in this department is bound by Peru's national framework. The parent framework is mixed. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The operative restriction on public facilities was approved in stages during 2025. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody and situations where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signage. The plenary of Congress approved the fused text on Wednesday 2 April 2025 as Article 5.1 of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes and waived a second vote. The stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

The Pontifical Catholic University of Peru's human-rights institute IDEHPUCP reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement would fall to security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

Enforcement already reaches private life. The consumer-protection body INDECOPI dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit under SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana Maria Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to go use the men's room.

Violence figures are national and rising, and recorded totals are a floor rather than a count. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 assassinations of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, with trans women most affected. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, and in 13 of the 19 killings in 2023. The observatory's co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One documented case illustrates the pattern of abduction and killing: in February 2023 the 31-year-old trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano was kidnapped from central Lima by the Los Gallegos extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot. Two killers were arrested in March 2023.

Hate-crime machinery does not reach these offences. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan Leon, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marin, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the bathroom provision is argued to violate. A Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional in July 2025.

After the 2017 repeal, Peru stands as one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. The repealing vote came after an April Constitutional Committee decision and a petition claiming one million signatures.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The airport complaint that prompted the 2025 bills concerned restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport rather than any facility in Lambayeque, so the legislative trigger arose outside this department while its effect is national.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, which shapes what documents a resident of Lambayeque can present to authorities, employers or venues. Where a venue assigns restrooms by the sex recorded in the DNI, as SmartFit did, a resident's access turns on that record rather than on presentation.

Health guidance for gender-diverse patients was updated in June 2024 when national health authorities removed pathologising terminology, which affects care settings residents attend in this department. Whether clinics and hospitals in Lambayeque have applied the revised terminology is not established by these sources.

Because sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from the state's crime-registration systems, a resident reporting an anti-trans attack in Lambayeque cannot have it registered or prosecuted as a hate crime; homicide and assault figures for the department are not broken down by anti-LGBTI motive.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory mentions Lambayeque, Chiclayo or any locality within the department. Absence of local material is unresolved rather than a finding that no incidents have occurred there; the department has simply not been researched here.

Whether municipal authorities, regional health facilities or private venues in Lambayeque enforce the April 2025 restroom rule, and how DNI checks are carried out in practice locally, is not sourced. The only documented enforcement example concerns a gym chain and a Lima consumer-protection resolution.

The 2020-2023 homicide and violation counts are national totals from one university observatory and are not disaggregated by department, so no Lambayeque figure can be derived from them. The co-author's warning that the data are a sub-registry makes the national totals themselves incomplete.

The article reporting the February 2025 dictamen and the IDEHPUCP legal analysis both contain no Lambayeque-specific content; the department's scoring rests on the national framework alone.
